questions.stem:
A 42-year-old man had a flu-like illness that over several weeks progressed to worsening shortness of breath. A lung biopsy is examined. Giemsa and silver stains show large round yeast forms, several of which have a single daughter cell attached across a wide, flat connection to the parent cell. No hyphae are seen.

Which organism produces this appearance?
choices: Cryptococcus neoformans
Blastomyces dermatitidis
Coccidioides immitis spherules
Aspergillus niger
Histoplasma capsulatum

explain.html:
Several yeasts appear in the case set, and the way they bud is what separates them. Blastomyces dermatitidis is a large round yeast with a single daughter cell attached across a broad base, easy to see on Giemsa and silver stains. Cryptococcus buds on a narrow base and carries a capsule. Histoplasma is small and sits inside macrophages. Coccidioides does not bud in tissue at all, since it forms spherules. Blastomycosis is acquired by inhaling spores and mainly involves the lung.

This man had a flu-like illness that progressed over weeks to respiratory distress, and his lung biopsy shows large yeast with wide, flat bud attachments and no hyphae. That broad-based budding identifies Blastomyces.

why: Cryptococcus buds on a narrow base and has a thick capsule.
Coccidioides forms thick-walled spherules with endospores, not budding yeast.
Aspergillus is a mold with septate hyphae, and no hyphae are seen here.
Histoplasma yeast is small and found inside macrophages.
explain.takeaway: Large yeast with a single broad-based bud in lung tissue identify Blastomyces dermatitidis.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize the gross and microscopic morphology associated with various fungal organisms and correlate this morphology with the clinical presentation of each disease

questions.stem:
A pathology laboratory processes four specimens from different patients. For specimen 1 a silver stain of lung tissue outlines fungal walls in dark brown against a pale background. For specimen 2 a drop of cerebrospinal fluid is mixed with a particulate ink and examined wet. Specimen 3 is a bone marrow aspirate stained with a Romanowsky-type stain. Specimen 4 is a skin biopsy stained with periodic acid-Schiff.

Which statement about these methods is correct?
choices: The particulate ink stains the organism itself a dark color
The silver method outlines fungal walls in tissue
The marrow stain cannot show organisms inside phagocytes
Periodic acid-Schiff stains only bacterial peptidoglycan
All four methods require viable organisms to be useful

explain.html:
The case set uses several stains, and each shows the fungus in its own way. Silver stains (GMS) outline fungal cell walls in dark brown to black against a pale background, so they are the standard way to find both yeast and hyphae in tissue sections. India ink is a negative stain: ink particles cannot enter the capsule, so the organism looks light on a dark field. Wright-Giemsa, a Romanowsky-type stain, shows yeast inside phagocytes on marrow and blood films. Periodic acid-Schiff highlights carbohydrate in fungal walls, staining them magenta in tissue.

Of the statements offered, only the one about silver outlining fungal walls in tissue is correct.
explain.table:
StainWhat it showsCase example
Silver (GMS)Fungal walls dark against a pale backgroundLung biopsies, marrow yeast
India inkNegative stain; capsule seen as a clear haloCryptococcus in spinal fluid
Wright-GiemsaYeast inside phagocytesHistoplasma in bone marrow
Periodic acid-SchiffFungal wall carbohydrate in tissueCandida esophagitis, mucormycosis
why: India ink is a negative stain, so the organism stays light and is not darkened.
Wright-Giemsa is exactly how intracellular yeast are seen on a marrow aspirate.
Periodic acid-Schiff highlights carbohydrate in fungal walls, not bacterial peptidoglycan.
These are morphologic stains and work on organisms that are no longer alive.
explain.takeaway: Silver and periodic acid-Schiff stains show fungal walls in tissue, India ink is a negative stain that reveals a capsule, and Wright-Giemsa shows yeast inside phagocytes.
explain.topic: Stains used to show fungi in tissue

explain.objective: Recognize the gross and microscopic morphology associated with various fungal organisms and correlate this morphology with the clinical presentation of each disease

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man with Hodgkin lymphoma recently treated with combination chemotherapy has fever, severe headaches, and new seizures. Cerebrospinal fluid is obtained. A Giemsa-stained preparation shows round cells of varying size with narrow-based budding, and an India ink preparation of the same fluid shows a wide unstained zone surrounding each cell.

Which morphologic feature in this preparation most directly establishes the diagnosis?
choices: Clusters of small cells inside leukocytes
Thick-walled structures packed with endospores
Hyphae with regular cross walls
The wide unstained zone around each cell
A single bud attached across a wide base

explain.html:
The skill in these cases is to read the morphology first and then match it to the organism and the clinical picture. Cryptococcus is a round yeast of varying size with narrow-based budding and a thick polysaccharide capsule. An India ink preparation is a negative stain: the ink particles cannot enter the capsule, so the capsule shows as a wide unstained halo around each cell. A Giemsa stain shows the yeast but does not set it apart from other round cells nearly as well. The halo is therefore the single finding that makes the diagnosis.

This man had chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma, which weakens cell-mediated immunity, and now has fever, severe headache and seizures. Haloed yeast in the cerebrospinal fluid places the infection in the central nervous system.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old missionary recently back from Central America has fever, weight loss, pancytopenia, and altered mental status, with an enlarged liver and spleen. A Wright-Giemsa stained bone marrow aspirate shows many small oval cells clustered inside mononuclear cells, and a silver stain of the same aspirate highlights the same small forms.

These findings are most consistent with which organism?
choices: Sporothrix schenckii
Rhizopus species
Blastomyces species
Aspergillus fumigatus
Histoplasma capsulatum

explain.html:
On a bone marrow aspirate, small fungal forms can sit inside host cells, and their size and location give the diagnosis. Histoplasma capsulatum appears as many small oval yeast packed inside macrophages. A Wright-Giemsa stain shows them within the cytoplasm, and a silver stain outlines the same small forms in black. Because the yeast multiplies inside macrophages, it travels to the marrow, liver and spleen. That spread explains the pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly of disseminated disease.

This returning missionary has fever, weight loss, falling counts, an enlarged liver and spleen and confusion, and the marrow shows exactly this intracellular pattern. No other organism in the case set looks like small yeast inside macrophages.

questions.stem:
A 60-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes presents with a rapidly developing facial lesion involving the nose and cheek, with dark discolored dead tissue at its center. A biopsy stained with periodic acid-Schiff shows broad, irregular, ribbon-like hyphae that lack cross walls and branch at wide angles. The lesion has expanded noticeably over 48 hours.

Which feature of the biopsy best distinguishes this organism from the other common mold causing invasive disease?
choices: Absence of septa and wide-angle branching
Presence of budding yeast alongside the hyphae
A thick capsule surrounding each hypha
Arthrospores forming along the filaments
Pigmented granules within the tissue

explain.html:
Two molds cause most invasive mold disease, and the biopsy tells them apart by the shape of the hyphae. The agents of mucormycosis form broad, irregular, ribbon-like hyphae that have no septa and branch at wide, near right angles. Aspergillus forms narrower, uniform hyphae with regular septa and acute-angle branching. Mucormycosis classically strikes patients with poorly controlled diabetes and spreads fast, leaving black, dead tissue.

This woman has poorly controlled diabetes and a facial lesion with a necrotic center that grew noticeably in 48 hours. The PAS-stained biopsy shows aseptate ribbon-like hyphae with wide branching, which is what separates the mucormycosis agents from Aspergillus.
explain.table:
FeatureMucormycosis agentsAspergillus
SeptaAbsentPresent
BranchingWide (right) anglesAcute (45 degree) angles
Hyphal shapeBroad, ribbon-like, irregularNarrow, uniform
Classic host in the casesPoorly controlled diabetesTransplant or leukemia
why: Budding yeast beside the hyphae would suggest Candida, not a mold invading tissue.
Hyphae do not carry a capsule; a capsule belongs to the yeast Cryptococcus.
Arthrospores form on Coccidioides filaments in soil, not in this tissue.
Granules belong to the branching bacteria Nocardia and Actinomyces, not to these two molds.
explain.takeaway: Broad, aseptate, ribbon-like hyphae branching at wide angles identify mucormycosis and separate it from septate, acute-angle Aspergillus.

explain.objective: Recognize the gross and microscopic morphology associated with various fungal organisms and correlate this morphology with the clinical presentation of each disease

questions.stem:
A previously healthy 35-year-old woman has low-grade fever, cough, and chest pain. A chest radiograph shows a single nodule in the left upper lobe. Her symptoms began about 3 weeks after she returned from a trip through the Sonoran Desert. Lung biopsy stained with hematoxylin and eosin and with silver shows large round thick-walled structures, some containing many small round bodies inside them.

How is this organism acquired?
choices: Contact with pigeon droppings during demolition
Spread along lymphatics from a distant abscess
Inhalation of arthrospores from dry soil
Ingestion of contaminated water
Inoculation of the organism into a skin wound

explain.html:
Coccidioides looks different in soil and in the body, and the tissue form is distinctive. In tissue it forms large, thick-walled spherules packed with many small endospores, which H&E and silver stains both show well, often within granulomas. In soil it grows as filaments that break into arthrospores. When dry desert soil is disturbed, the arthrospores become airborne and are inhaled, so infection begins in the lung. A primary infection can appear weeks after exposure as fever, cough and chest pain, sometimes with a solitary nodule.

This woman fell ill about 3 weeks after a trip through the Sonoran Desert, has a single upper lobe nodule, and her biopsy shows spherules with endospores. All of that points to inhaled arthrospores.

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man with multiple risk factors for immunosuppression has increasing difficulty swallowing with pain on swallowing. Endoscopy shows white plaques lining the esophagus, and his tongue is coated with similar white material that can be scraped off. A biopsy stained with periodic acid-Schiff shows budding yeast together with elongated chains of cells that remain attached end to end.

The elongated attached chains in this biopsy are best described as which structure?
choices: Pseudohyphae formed by budding yeast cells
Arthrospores released from filaments
Endospores escaping a spherule
Sporangiospores held within a sac
Septate true hyphae of a mold

explain.html:
Candida grows on mucosal surfaces as budding yeast, and when it invades it also forms pseudohyphae. Pseudohyphae are chains of elongated budding cells that stay attached end to end, pinched at each junction. True hyphae of a mold have continuous walls divided by septa. On a PAS-stained mucosal biopsy, budding yeast together with pseudohyphae is the pattern that sets Candida apart from the molds and the dimorphic fungi. Clinically it shows up as white plaques on the tongue and esophagus with painful swallowing.

This man has risk factors for immunosuppression, white material on the tongue that scrapes off, esophageal plaques, and a biopsy with budding yeast plus attached elongated chains. Those chains are pseudohyphae.

questions.stem:
Two patients with hematologic disease develop pulmonary infiltrates. Patient 1 has been profoundly neutropenic for 3 weeks after induction chemotherapy and has hemoptysis; biopsy shows narrow hyphae with regular cross walls branching at acute angles, invading vessel walls. Patient 2 has lymphoma treated with chemotherapy and presents with headache and seizures; the cerebrospinal fluid shows round cells with a wide clear zone on a negative stain.

Which pairing of host defect to organism is correct?
choices: Both infections follow inhalation of arthrospores from desert soil
Neither organism requires an immune defect to invade tissue
Neutropenia with Cryptococcus, impaired cell-mediated immunity with Aspergillus
Neutropenia with Aspergillus, impaired cell-mediated immunity with Cryptococcus
Both infections are explained by loss of the skin barrier

explain.html:
The host's immune defect predicts which fungal form turns up, and these two cases show the contrast. Aspergillus forms narrow septate hyphae with acute-angle branching and invades blood vessels. Its classic setting is prolonged, profound neutropenia, as after induction chemotherapy or bone marrow transplant, with hemoptysis from infarcted lung. Cryptococcus is a round yeast whose capsule leaves a wide clear zone on a negative stain. It disseminates to the central nervous system when cell-mediated immunity fails, as in lymphoma treated with chemotherapy.

Patient 1, neutropenic with hemoptysis and vessel-invading septate hyphae, has invasive aspergillosis. Patient 2, with lymphoma, headache, seizures and haloed yeast in the CSF, has cryptococcal meningitis.

Impaired cell-mediated immunityCryptococcusEncapsulated yeast, halo on India inkHeadache, seizures, meningitis
why: Inhaled desert arthrospores are the route for Coccidioides, which forms spherules, not these forms.
Both organisms cause invasive disease mainly in impaired hosts.
This reverses the two host defects.
Neither infection started at a skin wound; both began with inhalation.
explain.takeaway: Invasive aspergillosis follows prolonged neutropenia, while disseminated cryptococcosis follows impaired cell-mediated immunity.
